newsitem.title: USA: COFFEE -- Surprise stock draw should boost prices.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE -- Surprise stock draw should boost prices.

text.p: U.S. coffee stocks certified for delivery at the Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange fell sharply last week, surprising traders and setting the stage for a futures market rally tomorrow, industry sources said.
Supplies of coffee in exchange-certified warehouses fell by 10,433 60-kg bags on the week, the CSCE reported after the close of business on Monday, to 31,669 bags.
Traders said the drawdown, which appeared to catch many operators by surprise, would likely give a boost to prices when trading resumes on Tuesday.
"It's relatively constructive," said one. "I don't think that anyone was looking for that big of a drawdown."
"This is going to help the New York market a bit, especially after bouncing off the low (at 102.25) today."
The drawdown reduced the CSCE stockpile to at least a 10-year low, analysts said, although exact historical comparisons were not immediately available from the exchange.
Equally important, traders said, was the absence of coffee awaiting certification, or approval, at exchange warehouses.
"There is absolutely nothing pending, which is even more constructive," said one.

Had the trading ring gotten wind of the drawdown ahead of time, dealers said, it was unlikely the market would have sold off as sharply as it had today. New York's benchmark December contract slumped 2.30 cents per lb on Monday, to 102.95 cents, its lowest close in nearly two months.

Although traders described today's swift sell-off as primarily chart-driven, noting that the slide halted at crucial support levels, it drew the market closer to a test of of the widely-watched 100-cent ($1) per pound mark.

But the certified stock data, coming at the start of the 1996/97 harvest in key Latin American producing countries, could reverse the trend and bolster December's already steep premium to the outer months.
At Monday's close, December stood at a 3.45-cent premium to second-position March, reflecting views that coffee would be widely available by early 1997.
"It's very good for the switch," said one. "Tomorrow we're probably going to see the nearby spread go back out to perhaps 6.00 cents."

Traders speculated that the bulk of the coffee that left the Exchange warehouses last week ended up in the hands of one or more roasters. In recent weeks, the processing sector has been a steady buyer of the futures market at the lows, helping to stave off what many traders feel is an inevitable slide back to the 90-100 cent range not seen since last January.

December futures would need to challenge resistance at 105 and 107.25 cents to signal a new uptrend, chartists said. Further upside barriers awaited at 108-110 cents, while sell stops were reportedly placed from 102.25 to 101.50.
